sources.title: Photography Certification Guide, Module 1E: Lens Selection
sources.author: Jessica Avery (PPA page editor); Professional Photographers of America
sources.identity: Professional photographers' association certification curriculum
sources.trust_reason: PPA publishes a public certification guide for professional photographers; the complete module is readable and identifies its editor.
sources.read_depth: Read complete module, including definitions and comparison of lens families. It describes compression as a telephoto property; reconcile that simplified wording with viewpoint-controlled geometry sources before using as a formal claim.
sources.notes: Useful framework and professional curriculum coverage. Its statements about lens 'distortion' and compression are simplified and need triangulation; do not elevate the implied fixed focal-length rule into universal portrait advice.

sources.title: Photography Certification Guide, Module 1F: Capabilities of Lenses

sources.identity: Professional photographers' association certification curriculum

sources.read_depth: Read complete module, including depth-of-field factors, perspective convergence, portrait crop-specific camera-height suggestions, and hyperfocal examples.
sources.notes: Directly distinguishes camera height from keeping the lens level to the ground for full-length, two-thirds, and head-and-shoulders examples. Numerical DoF rules in this text should be checked against current optical references and format/focus conditions.

sources.title: Perspective Distortion in Photographic Composition
sources.author: Todd Vorenkamp
sources.identity: B&H eXplora photography educator/editor; named author at professional photo retailer
sources.trust_reason: Named photography educator's technical article, with diagrams and examples, published by a long-running professional photo retailer.
sources.read_depth: Read the complete article, including distinction between optical and perspective distortion and its angle discussion.
sources.notes: Useful counterweight to simplistic 'wide lens distorts' advice. The article's statement that telephotos optically compress is overbroad; the camera viewpoint changes when photographers back up to maintain framing. Reconcile via controlled viewpoint comparisons and the vision-science paper.

sources.title: Camera Focal Length and the Perception of Pictures
sources.author: Martin S. Banks, Emily A. Cooper, and Elise A. Piazza
sources.identity: Peer-reviewed vision-science researchers at UC Berkeley; published in Ecological Psychology
sources.trust_reason: Primary research article authored by university vision scientists and published in a peer-reviewed perception journal; public full-text PDF is hosted by a coauthor's university page.
sources.independence_key: Banks, Cooper, and Piazza research group
sources.read_depth: Opened the full 19-page PDF and scanned the experimental setup and discussion. The study varies focal length and camera distance under different controls; use the relevant experimental condition rather than flatten its nuanced findings into 'lens never matters'.
sources.notes: Strong source for teasing apart image projection and viewer-perceived compression. It is not a portrait posing manual and does not prescribe a universally ideal working focal length.

gaps: Height versus pitch is now directly distinguished across a university cinematography text, PPA curriculum, and portrait practice sources. A controlled still-portrait comparison of roll versus pitch and the expressive effects of low height versus upward tilt remains thin; no universal low-angle emotion rule is supported.

Viewpoint-controlled focal-length perception is represented by a peer-reviewed experiment, with a photographer’s same-position focal-length series. A second independent portrait study that holds camera-to-subject distance and framing under explicit controls would improve triangulation; terminology like “telephoto compression” remains inconsistent across sources.

Near-object scale and lean/foreshortening now have several opened portrait sources, but no opened source directly studies cosplay props or oversize costume components. Any prop-specific practice remains an adaptation to verify in field work.

Shot-scale terms have textbook support and professional portrait examples, but an open, independent named portrait teacher’s deliberate one-session coverage sequence was not found at the same detail level. Do not treat Tamron’s generic shot list as consensus.

Depth-of-field factors and eye-focus priorities are represented. Source-backed tradeoffs for multiple-depth cosplay costume/prop details, subject movement, tracking reliability, and focus plane are incomplete; camera-specific AF behavior needs body-specific testing.
Canon official lens knowledge pages remained index-only after a direct 502. Nikon College remains a course listing and cannot support detailed technique claims.

No source in this pass supports cosplay-specific rules for large swords, daggers, wigs, wide sleeves, or convention-space constraints. Candidate practices use generic portrait geometry and label cosplay applications as project adaptations.
